blocks.text: Next we must speak of honey, which Scripture mentions in many places. In Hebrew honey is [col. 518] called דבש debas, an ambiguous name, by which dates are also designated. Kimchi in his Lexicon: ונקראו התמרים דבש, They also called dates DEBAS (that is, honey). R. Selomo and the same Kimchi wish it to be taken in this way in 2 Paral. XXXI, 6., where the Israelites are said to have offered the first fruits of grain, of must and of oil, ודבש, and of debas, that is, they say, of dates. Kimchi adds that the ancients took it thus in Deut. VIII, 8., in which passage God promises that He will bring him into a land זית שמן ודבש, of oil-bearing olives and of debas. To this point belongs the fact that in Alcamus دبوس [dabūs] dubous are خلاص تمر يلقي في مسلاء السمن فيذوب فيه [khalāṣ tamr yulqā fī maslāʾ al-samn fa-yadhūbu fīhi] choicer dates, which are thrown into melted butter, so as to dissolve in it. And دبس [dibs] dibs, or dibis, is غسل التمر وغسل النخل [ghasl al-tamr wa-ghasl al-nakhl] the honey of the date and the honey of the palm, that is, the juice of the date or of the palm. It rightly shares its name with honey, since its taste is similar. Josephus, The Jewish War, book 5, chapter 3, speaking of the valley of Jericho: It produces most beautiful and very dense gardens, and many kinds of irrigated palms, varying both in taste and in names. Τούτων οἱ πιότεροι πατούμενοι, καὶ μέλι δαψιλὲς ἀνίασιν, οὐ πολλῷ τοῦ λοιποῦ χεῖρον· [Toutōn hoi pioteroi patoumenoi, kai meli dapsiles aniasin, ou pollō tou loipou cheiron] The richest of these, when trodden, give out a great deal of honey, not much inferior to other honey. And another Josephus, closer in time indeed but more remote in place, namely the Indian, in his Voyage, chapter 138: In the month of August the Indians prune the palm. And since the trees are then at their most luxuriant, when cut they groan, and emit tears like a wounded vine. These they catch in vessels for only three days after the tree has been wounded, etc. But whoever wishes to make sugar, let him take water of this kind flowing out within three days, and put it in copper pots and boil it, until scarcely a third part remains. Then, thus boiled down, it becomes a most sweet honey. It is therefore clear why the Hebrews gave the name of honey either to dates or to the juice of the palm ^{(1)}. Indeed R. Selomo on Levit. II, 11. extends it much more widely, as though דבש debas meant כל מתיקת פרי, all sweetness of fruit ^{(2)}. However that may be, here we are dealing with honey properly so called.
